newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia and Poland put economics before NATO row.
newsitem.headline: Russia and Poland put economics before NATO row.

text.p: Poland and Russia signed a range of economic agreements on Wednesday, demonstrating a willingness to strengthen ties despite differences over Warsaw's efforts to join NATO and the European Union.

The deals, signed on the second of a four-day visit to Russia by Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, covered trade liberalisation and a settlement of communist-era mutual trade debts, Russian news agencies said.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said the agreements had been four years in the making. "What we have done today is of crucial importance for our economic cooperation," Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying.
Relations between the former Warsaw pact allies have been strained by Poland's bid to join NATO despite Russian fears that expansion of the Western defence alliance might threaten its own security.
But the two delegations made sure that differences over NATO did not get in the way of their economic relations.
"The two sides touched on the question of NATO expansion, but limited their discussion to a restatement of the known opinions of Poland and Russian on this issue and an exchange of views," Tass said.

Cimoszewicz said investment and banking cooperation had also played an important part in the negotiations as had efforts to boost the fight against organised crime, which has grown with post-communist political and economic liberalisation.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Davydov said the details of the agreement on mutual debts, which date back to the 1980s when the two countries were in the now-defunct Comecon trade bloc, would be filled in by a working group.
"We must not drag this out," Interfax quoted Chernomyrdin as saying.
He said bilateral trade had increased this year by more than $1 billion, to $4 billion.
"But we could do even more," Interfax quoted him as saying. "Both of our economies have enormous potential and we have got to move forward quickly."

Davydov said the trade liberalisation deal paved the way for a free trade zone, although Warsaw has said that this would be difficult given Poland's desire to move towards full membership of the European Union.
Chernomyrdin said Russia did not mind Warsaw's moves towards the European Union but that the process should not impair its trade with Moscow.

Tass said the two delegations also had confidential discussions on possible joint military production for export to third countries and signed agreements on joint air and sea search and rescue and cultural cooperation for next year.
Cimoszewicz was later due to meet officials and businessmen in St Petersburg before flying to Tatarstan, the autonomous region in central Russia, to discuss possible oil imports.
